newsitem.title: USA: Seagram chief Bronfman testifies in Viacom battle.
newsitem.headline: Seagram chief Bronfman testifies in Viacom battle.

text.p: Seagram Co. Ltd. Chief Executive Edgar Bronfman Jr. testified Monday he had no choice but to sue Viacom Inc. after its Chairman Sumner Redstone sought additional concessions in return for allowing former Viacom executive Frank Biondi to join MCA.

In testimony in Delaware Chancery Court, Bronfman said he originally agreed not to sue Viacom over the company's launch of "Nick at Nite TV Land" if Viacom released Biondi from a one-year clause that barred him from working for a competitor.

Bronfman said, however, that he changed his mind when Redstone allegedly tried to extend the understanding to include a blanket waiver of the partnership provision barring the companies from establishing competing cable operations.

Viacom, which owns Paramount Pictures, MTV and Nickelodeon, and Seagram, the Montreal-based beverage firm that owns entertainment and theme park concern MCA Inc., have been fighting for control of their jointly-owned USA Network cable channel, with each side accusing the other of violating the terms of their partnership agreement.
The case was put on hold last week to give both sides an opportunity to reach a settlement but the talks fell through, forcing the companies to return to court.
According to Bronfman, Redstone's response to a lawsuit was, "If you want a war Edgar, you've got one."

Bronfman testified that in March he suggested to Redstone that MCA could buy Viacom's half of the partnership or they could divide the assets with USA Network going to MCA and Sci- Fi network to Viacom.
According to Bronfman, Redstone said one network "earns a lot of money and the other (Sci-Fi) loses money. You want to offer $5 billion, I'll think about it."

The USA cable network broadcasts a variety of programs ranging from re-runs of "Murder, She Wrote" to original movies and the U.S. Open tennis tournament. The less popular Sci-Fi channel is known for broadcasting re-runs of "Lost in Space" and "The Twilight Zone."
Bronfman said Redstone also pointed out that Viacom would have to pay "an enormous tax if we sell our cable interest."

Bronfman said when he told former MCA chief Lou Wasserman that he was not getting anyplace with Redstone and would have to sue, Wasserman replied, "Well Edgar, that's the only language Sumner understands."
MCA is expected to conclude its case when Bronfman's testimony is completed Tuesday. Viacom will then begin its counterclaim lawsuit with Redstone as its first witness, possibly not until Wednesday.

Vice Chancellor Myron Steele has scheduled four weeks for the trial which began Oct 15. In comments to attorneys Monday he indicated there was "an expectation of an opinion within days" of the trial's conclusion around Nov. 14.
Seagram filed suit against Viacom in April, charging the company with violating the terms of the partnership agreement by launching "Nick at Nite TV Land."
Seagram said the partnership prevents either company from operating or launching entertainment cable networks outside of the USA Network.
Viacom contends, however, that there is no breach of the partnership, that the partnership is working well and that MCA is trying to get control of USA Network at an unfairly low price.

USA Network, which reaches 65 million homes, was launched in 1981 by MCA, Paramount Pictures and Time Inc. Time eventually sold out to the partners. In 1994, Paramount was acquired by Viacom and a year later Seagram acquired MCA.

The battle between Viacom and Seagram is expected to put current MCA Chairman Frank Biondi in a difficult situation because as the former chief executive for Viacom, Biondi had argued the launch of "TV Land" was not a violation of the partnership agreement.
